extracted.intended_audience: aspiring novelists, critics, and students of fiction
extracted.subtask_description: Practical and aesthetic guidance on writing novels, covering characterization (flat vs round), point of view, interiority, and the nature and construction of plot. Emphasises tests and techniques a novelist can use to create convincing characters and coherent, affecting plots.

rubrics_metrics.name: Flat characters
rubrics_metrics.description: Flat characters (also called 'humours', 'types', or 'caricatures') are constructed round a single idea or quality and can often be expressed in one sentence (e.g. “I never will desert Mr. Micawber”).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advantages: easily recognized by the reader, need no reintroduction, provide a ready atmosphere, are easily remembered and lend permanence to a work. Useful as comic elements and as conveniences for the author (they 'provide their own atmosphere—little luminous disks of a pre-arranged size'). Disadvantages/anti-patterns: if used seriously or tragically they bore; flattening in biography falsifies complexity; overuse can produce falsity of life. Examples: Mrs. Micawber, Caleb Balderstone, Princess of Parma, many Dickens and Wells characters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Round characters
rubrics_metrics.description: Round characters cannot be summed up in a single phrase; they possess complexity and the 'incalculability of life' and are capable of change, development, and surprising behaviour.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Round characters are necessary for sustained tragedy and deep emotional movement. Test: 'The test of a round character is whether it is capable of surprising in a convincing way.' If a character never surprises, or if its surprises do not convince, it is effectively flat. Examples: principal characters in War and Peace, Dostoevsky figures, Madame Bovary, Becky Sharp, Lucy Snowe.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use a mixture of flat and round characters
rubrics_metrics.description: Novels often require both flat and round characters; flat people can be used together with round ones to achieve desired effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A skilful novelist combines types and complexity so that flat characters never seem merely mechanical; their recurrence helps give structure and permanence while round characters supply depth. Examples: Dickens and Wells use many flat types but transmit 'force' so they appear alive; Jane Austen's characters, though sometimes labelable, function 'all round' and can extend into roundness when needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character must be credible when extended
rubrics_metrics.description: Characters should be capable of surviving unforeseen events (an 'extended life') and of revealing new sides under pressure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A character that can be expanded convincingly by plot events (e.g., Lady Bertram modulated into roundness in response to crisis) demonstrates authorial control and verisimilitude. If a character collapses or becomes inconsistent under incident, the novel's probability is weakened.

rubrics_metrics.name: Point of view / narrator relation to story
rubrics_metrics.description: Decide the narrator's relation to the story: describe from outside as an onlooker, assume omniscience, inhabit a character (dramatic/internal), or choose intermediate attitudes; shifts among these are possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The essential power is the writer's ability to 'bounce the reader into accepting what he says.' Shifting point of view is permissible and can be an advantage (as in Dickens and Tolstoy) if it 'comes off' and is not conspicuous; over-attention to method or self-conscious jolts can make a work merely interesting rather than vital (Gide's example). Examples: Bleak House (shifts between omniscience, partial omniscience, and dramatized first person), Les Faux Monnayeurs (sophisticated shifting), War and Peace (effective intermittent omniscience).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid taking the reader into your confidence about individual characters
rubrics_metrics.description: Authorial confidences about individual people (''Let’s think of why B does that—perhaps there’s more in him...'' ) are dangerous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such confidences tend to cool the creative state, lead to intellectual and emotional laxity, facetiousness, and bar-parlour chatty analysis; they beckon the reader away from the characters to an examination of the novelist's mind. Distinguish this from general confidences about the universe or social conditions, which are less harmful (Hardy and Conrad draw back and generalize successfully).

rubrics_metrics.name: Novelist's privilege: access to the secret life / interiority
rubrics_metrics.description: A novel's special ability is to reveal the secret life—the private, interior states and subconscious—that drama cannot show.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The novelist can present soliloquy, subconscious processes short-circuiting into action, and internal motivation. The primary criterion is whether such presentation is convincing; questions about shifting standpoint are secondary if the interior portrayal works for the reader.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plot vs story — plot as causality
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguish story (narrative of events in time sequence) from plot (narrative emphasizing causality—asking 'why?' rather than merely 'and then').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plot suspends time-sequence to create causality and mystery; it demands intelligence and memory from the reader and cannot be reduced to mere curiosity (the 'and then—and then' audience). Examples: a story is 'The king died and then the queen died.' A plot is 'The queen died of grief at the king's death.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Plot requires intelligence and memory in the reader
rubrics_metrics.description: A plot presumes an intelligent reader who picks up facts, relates them to earlier material, and broods on partial information; it also presumes memory so that clues and correspondences are retained.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Curiosity alone is insufficient for plot appreciation. The intelligent reader mentally stores facts both in isolation and in relation to previous facts; the novel may build cross-correspondences whose full meaning emerges later. If the reader forgets earlier material, the plot will fail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mystery and suspension of chronology are essential plot devices
rubrics_metrics.description: Mystery (a 'pocket in time') and the suspension of chronological sequence create the detective/ suspense element necessary to a plot.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mystery allows parts of the mind to remain brooding while the rest proceeds; the novelist uses half-explained gestures and delayed revelation to build causal chains and aesthetic compactness. A good plot uses mystery without misleading, preserving organic development.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economy, coherence, and avoid dead matter in plot
rubrics_metrics.description: Every action or word in the plot ought to count; plot should be economical, spare, organic, and free from dead matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Loose ends and unnecessary material weaken plot. Even complex plots must avoid misleading the reader; the final sense should feel aesthetically compact and earned by earlier material. Beauty in plot arises when these conditions are met (though a novelist should not aim at beauty as a forced objective).

rubrics_metrics.name: Plot should produce surprise and transform characters
rubrics_metrics.description: A well-constructed plot causes genuine surprise and produces consequential transformations in characters and their world.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contrivances can be artfully placed to create shocks that alter the book's personages (Meredith's 'contrivances' like the horse‑whipping episode). The shock followed by the reconciliatory feeling 'Oh, that's all right' signals a plot working well: characters remain credible while incidents produce unexpected effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: The novelist must 'bounce' the reader—make technical shifts acceptable
rubrics_metrics.description: The novelist's power to make readers accept shifts in viewpoint, method, or control ('bounce us') is central to aesthetic success.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even when the work is 'all to pieces logically' (shifting viewpoints), the reader will forgive technical looseness if the authorial energy or technique persuades. Conversely, if the novelist draws attention to method, it often reduces emotional temperature and pleasure.
